source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30)
finding: Canadian strategic intelligence unit forecasts were highly discriminating and well calibrated.
numbers: 1,514 forecasts (from 1,943 numeric; Mar 2005-Dec 2011). ROC area 0.940 (SE 0.007). Mean Brier 0.074. Calibration index 0.016. About 94% classified correctly. Forecasts explained 76% of outcome variance.
quote: Both discrimination and calibration of forecasts was very good.
limits: Single organisation. Outcomes coded by the authors; ambiguous ones needed judgement. Questions mostly short horizon (see Tetlock and Mellers critique).
agent_relevance: Shows a human analyst pipeline can be scored. Gives a bar: Brier about 0.07 on short-horizon intelligence questions, far below the 0.25 no-skill line.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30): sensitivity of the headline
finding: Headline Brier rises but stays good when ambiguous outcomes and vague words are scored in less favourable ways.
numbers: Partial-credit coding of ambiguous outcomes: Brier 0.090. Coding unquantified words (could, might) as 0.50: Brier 0.097.
limits: Coding choices move the score by 0.016 to 0.023. Still far better than 0.25.
agent_relevance: Any agent scoring on free-text forecasts must fix a coding rule in advance; the rule alone shifts Brier by about a quarter.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30): miscalibration is underconfidence
finding: Analysts were underconfident, not overconfident. They gave more uncertainty than the evidence needed.
numbers: Signed calibration of confidence index -0.076 (99% CI -0.082 to -0.070).
quote: Miscalibration was mainly due to underconfidence such that analysts assigned more uncertainty than needed
limits: Contrasts with Tetlock (2005) overconfident experts; horizon, accountability and question mix differ.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model is overconfident. For a wrapped agent, measure direction of miscalibration first; a blanket 'be less sure' rule can flip it to underconfidence.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30): moderators
finding: Seniority and question difficulty moderated accuracy. Harder and more important questions drew more underconfidence.
numbers: Senior vs junior ROC area 0.951 vs 0.909 (Z=2.24, p=0.025). Easier vs harder 0.966 vs 0.913 (Z=3.57, p<0.001). Median underconfidence harder -0.106 vs easier -0.044 (Z=-13.39). Greater vs lesser importance -0.071 vs -0.044 (Z=-4.49). Time frame and importance had no effect on discrimination (p>0.25). Regression: difficulty b=1.26, importance b=0.32, pseudo-R2 0.124.
limits: Difficulty and importance were rated after the fact by raters, so hindsight can leak in. Seniority is confounded with case assignment.
agent_relevance: Expertise helped discrimination, not calibration. Hedging grows when stakes are high; an agent told the stakes are high may hedge more.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30): recalibration
finding: Remapping stated probabilities after the fact removes most miscalibration.
numbers: Karmarkar-style transform (a=2.2): calibration index 0.016 to 0.0018; mean absolute deviation from perfect calibration 12.7% to 4.2% (66.9% fall). Remapping to original scale points: 0.0021 and 4.6% (63.8% fall).
limits: Fitted on the same data it was scored on, so in-sample. Needs a stable track record.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side recalibration step (G5 style): map the model's stated numbers using its own track record rather than asking it to rethink.

source: Mandel and Barnes (2014) Accuracy of forecasts in strategic intelligence, PNAS 111(30): comparison with Tetlock 2005
finding: The authors claim analysts beat Tetlock's expert sample on variance explained and calibration.
numbers: Variance explained 76% vs about 20% for Tetlock's best political forecasters. Mean absolute calibration deviation about 25% smaller.
limits: Cross-study comparison. Tetlock and Mellers (2014) call it apples to oranges: different horizons, questions and incentives.
agent_relevance: Do not use cross-study Brier comparisons as proof of skill. Compare on the same question set.

source: Tetlock and Mellers (2014) Judging political judgment, PNAS commentary on Mandel and Barnes
finding: Main critique: easy questions, short horizons, and Brier symmetry make the 'analysts are great' claim hard to read. Brier scores are not comparable across question sets.
numbers: 59% of questions resolved within 6 months and 96% within 1 year. Over half of forecasts scored Brier 0 or 0.01. 55% of questions rated 'harder' in hindsight. IARPA tournament best teams reached similar Brier over similar horizons.
limits: A commentary by authors of the rival tournament; the critics have a stake.
agent_relevance: Question difficulty and horizon must be reported with any Brier. Use a fixed question set for A/B tests of the scaffold.

source: Tetlock and Mellers (2014): asymmetric blame and threshold shifting
finding: Brier counts over and under prediction equally, but real costs are asymmetric. After a visible miss, agencies tend to just shift the response threshold.
numbers: No numbers beyond the tournament cost contrast: about $5 million per year vs well over $5 billion for the intelligence community.
quote: In signal detection terms, you just shift your response threshold for crying wolf.
limits: Argument, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Choose the scoring rule to match the cost of a miss. Add a check for threshold shifting after any 'be careful' instruction.

source: Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Correcting judgment correctives in national security intelligence, Front Psychol
finding: Current tradecraft (structured analytic techniques, bias warnings) has never been validated against accuracy. Warnings against overconfidence may cause the mirror bias, underconfidence. Structured methods may add noise.
numbers: Cites underconfidence in strategic intelligence forecasts (Mandel and Barnes 2014, 2018) and in experimental tasks (Mandel 2015). Recalibration toward extremity helped in the IARPA ACE tournament (Baron et al. 2014; Turner et al. 2014).
limits: Position paper with hypotheses, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Backs G1: do not add generic doubt steps. Advocates post-hoc recalibration and averaging over analyst-side debiasing.

source: Mandel (2015) Instruction in information structuring improves Bayesian judgment in intelligence analysts, Front Psychol
finding: A short tutorial on natural-frequency trees made analyst probabilities more additive and closer to Bayes.
numbers: N=43 Canadian analysts, pre/post. Mean absolute bias larger for P(H|D) (M=0.144) than P(not-H|D) (M=0.009), F(1,42)=12.38, p=0.001. Instruction effect larger where bias was larger (F=6.67, p=0.013). Over four fifths gave additive answers on all 8 problems after instruction.
limits: No control group; immediate post-test; not a forecasting-accuracy outcome. Fifty-fifty blips may inflate additivity.
agent_relevance: Natural-frequency framing is a cheap, tested aid for the Bayes step. Have code enforce complement sums to 1 (G5).

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd et al. (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation, Cogn Res Princ Implic
finding: The ACH matrix layout did not reduce confirmation bias; putting hypotheses in rows did. Most military analysts showed no confirmation bias.
numbers: Study 1 N=161 students/staff; Study 2 N=62 Dutch military analysts. Coherence and cognitive reflection did not separate better from worse performers.
limits: Study 1 sample was young, 90% female students; Study 2 small. Abstract and design read; not every table.
agent_relevance: A standard analyst aid (ACH) lacks support in its common layout. Layout of evidence may matter more than the named method.

source: Mellers, McCoy, Lu and Tetlock (2024) Human and algorithmic predictions in geopolitical forecasting, Perspect Psychol Sci
finding: Review of IARPA tournaments: training, teaming and tracking each improved accuracy, and most gain came from less noise.
numbers: Training raised accuracy 6% to 11% per year vs untrained. Teams of about 10-15 beat independents in each of 4 years. Over 50% of gain from the three interventions was noise reduction (BIN model). Statistical vs human intuition d=0.12 (Grove et al. 2000).
limits: Written by the project authors; no new data; no N or Brier values in the text read.
agent_relevance: Noise reduction by aggregation is the main lever. Matches G4/G5: average samples, but samples from one model are correlated, so gain is smaller.

source: Mellers et al. (2015) Identifying and cultivating superforecasters, Perspect Psychol Sci 10(3)
finding: Top performers selected each year and teamed beat the rest. Four factors explain it: ability and style, task skill, motivation, enriched environment. Seen only through search snippets and later citations.
numbers: Training module about one hour with effects lasting at least a year (secondary summary). Forecasters used granular numbers; at least four distinct categories raised accuracy (as cited in Lu 2025).
limits: Not opened. Figures taken from secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness and time spent are traits we can only partly copy in a model; training in base rates and outside view can be copied as prompt content.

source: Friedman, Lerner, Zeckhauser et al. (2018) The value of precision in probability assessment, Int Stud Q 62(2)
finding: Rounding probabilities to coarse verbal-like categories consistently loses accuracy in a large geopolitical tournament.
numbers: 888,328 geopolitical forecasts. Loss held for extreme estimates, short horizons, different scoring rules.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. No numeric effect size seen.
agent_relevance: Do not collapse the agent's numbers into words like 'likely'. Keep numeric output; map words in code afterwards.

source: Shemesh, Gamoran, Leiser and Gilead (2025) Do people listen to Cassandra? Persuasion and accuracy in geopolitical forecasts, PSPB
finding: How persuasive a forecaster's written reason is does not predict how accurate the forecast is.
numbers: 153 forecasters, 474 raters, about 1,530 rationales, 10 Metaculus questions. Persuasion vs accuracy: forecast-level beta 0.007 (p=0.325, BF10 0.024); forecaster-level beta 0.04 (p=0.52). BERT read correctness at AUC 0.75. Confident style r=-0.02 with accuracy; insistent r=-0.38.
limits: Not preregistered. One 10-question contest. Sample 82% male. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Fluent rationale is not evidence of a good forecast. A judge reading the model's reasons will be fooled the same way (G5).

source: Zhu, Newall, Sundh, Chater and Sanborn (2022) Clarifying the relationship between coherence and accuracy in probability judgments, Cognition
finding: Coherent probability judgments go with accurate ones, between groups and within people, once the measures are not tied together. Earlier null results may be low power.
numbers: Exp 1: 82 retained (45 novices, 37 amateurs); Exp 2: 186 poker experts. Experts more coherent and accurate than pooled others (p<0.01). 25/30 correlations positive for novices, 16/30 amateurs, 27/30 experts; none negative. Inconsistency vs inaccuracy r=0.37 experts, 0.28 novices, 0.06 amateurs.
limits: Small-world tasks with known probabilities; 57 of 139 removed in Exp 1; experts 94% male. Authors did not test capacity as the cause.
agent_relevance: Incoherence is a usable cheap signal of error (a code check with no ground truth). Supports consistency checks for LLM forecasters.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han and Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval plus tuned reasoning plus ensembling got a language model close to, but not at, the human crowd on questions after its knowledge cutoff.
numbers: Test questions after 2023-06-01 from 5 platforms. System Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%). Best no-retrieval baseline GPT-4-1106 0.208; most of 14 models near or worse than 0.25. Weighted average of system and crowd 0.146.
limits: Brier SEs assume independence while data are time series, so error is understated. Pitfalls paper (Paleka et al. 2025) finds at least 3.8% of questions resolved early with no forecast needed.
agent_relevance: Raw models are not good forecasters; scaffolding (retrieval, aggregation) closes about 0.03 of a 0.06 gap. A scaffold effect with a measured size.

source: Halawi et al. (2024): where the LLM beats the crowd
finding: LLM beats the crowd only when the crowd is unsure, early in a question's life, and with many retrieved articles. Selective forecasting beats the crowd.
numbers: Crowd between .3 and .7: system .199 vs crowd .246. Crowd confident (near 0 or 1): crowd better; system accuracy 7% higher yet Brier .04 worse. All three conditions together: .240 vs .247 on 22% of forecasts, 43% of questions. Ablation: fine-tuned reasoner + retrieval .179; base GPT-4 no retrieval .206.
limits: Selection rules were found on validation then applied; small margins within error.
agent_relevance: The model hedges near 50% (safety-tuning guess by the authors), losing Brier on near-certain events. Code can push the model's number toward 0/1 only with a track record; and abstain where the model is weak.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park and Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd, Study 1
finding: An ensemble of 12 LLMs matched a human crowd on 31 questions, replicating the wisdom-of-crowds effect for models.
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs no-skill 0.25 (t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026); vs 925 human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), p=0.85; equivalence within 0.081. Singles: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4+Bing 0.16, Bard 0.19, Claude 2 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38. Model means above 50% (acquiescence).
limits: Only 31 questions, one 3-month tournament; the best single model (GPT-4, 0.15) was better than the ensemble average, so aggregation mostly protected against weak models. Not a large replication.
agent_relevance: Averaging a mixed pool is robust to bad members, but the pool here was different model families, not samples of one model (G4).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd, Study 2: exposure to the human median
finding: Showing a model the human median improved it, but simply averaging model and human was better.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001); accuracy gain 17% to 28%. Simple average with the human median: GPT-4 0.13, Claude 2 0.14; updated forecasts worse than the average (p=0.011 and p=0.001).
limits: Median human forecast known to the model; compared across 93 paired items.
agent_relevance: Combine in code, not in the model's head: the model's own update under-uses the anchor. Supports G5.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott and Tetlock (2024) AI-augmented predictions: LLM assistants improve human forecasting accuracy
finding: Human forecasters who consulted a GPT-4-Turbo assistant were more accurate than a control with a weak assistant, even when the assistant was deliberately biased.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Accuracy up 24% to 28% vs control (preregistered). Without one outlier question, superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%. Mean-of-medians error (excl. Q3): 0.11 good assistant, 0.28 noisy, 0.15 control.
limits: One outlier item changed the result; control model weaker than treatment, so it tests 'any strong LLM' not advice quality. Hypotheses that gains favour low skill or hurt crowd diversity were not consistently supported.
agent_relevance: A noisy advisor still helped on the preregistered measure, so benefit is not from calibrated numbers alone. Readers cannot easily tell good advice from bad (see Shemesh).

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: By mid-2025 a frontier reasoning model passed the cited crowd benchmark but remained far behind expert forecasters on a subset.
numbers: 464 Metaculus questions, 2 quarters. o3 Brier 0.1352 vs crowd 0.149 (Halawi) and 0.121 (Karger). Ten hired expert forecasters on 157 questions: mean Brier 0.1573, median 0.0225; held-out: mean 0.1222, median 0.0196. Narrative prompts worse than direct. Models better on politics than economics.
limits: Different question sets, so Brier not comparable across studies (the paper says so). Experts forecast about 31-47% of questions, chosen by them. Medians vs means differ a lot.
agent_relevance: Cross-study comparisons are weak. Experts picking their questions inflates their edge; an agent that can abstain should be scored the same way.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities, ICLR
finding: On a leakage-free rolling benchmark, top LLMs matched the public but trailed superforecasters.
numbers: 1,000 questions from nine sources. Superforecasters Brier 0.096 (0.076 on a combination-question table), public 0.121, top LLM on the 200-question subset (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 0.122; leaderboard top GPT-4o about 0.126-0.130. Gap superforecasters to GPT-4o 0.054, larger than GPT-4o to GPT-4 (0.026). Extrapolation: parity near Arena score 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Brier vs Arena r=-0.68.
limits: Extrapolation from 16 models with a wide interval. Public group was a survey with minimal forecasting experience; 39 superforecasters.
agent_relevance: Best current anchor for how far from expert level the model is, and a test that cannot be leaked. Use it as the external check for our scaffold.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: Reports that LLMs match human forecasters may be inflated by leakage and by badly built question sets.
numbers: At least 3.8% of Halawi et al. questions resolved early (no forecast needed); at least 10% of Tao et al. trivially forecastable; over 90% of a news-generated set rated unnatural; weak classifiers reach over 80% on that set. Date-restricted search engines still return post-date text.
limits: Counts are the authors' estimates, partly subjective. No new head-to-head forecasting run.
agent_relevance: Any gain we measure from the scaffold must be on questions that resolve after the model's cutoff and after our run date.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Logical consistency across related questions predicts later Brier score, giving an instant quality signal.
numbers: Arbitrage-based consistency scores correlate with Brier at 0.85 (one aggregate), 0.49 and 0.69 (others), and about 0.92 for conditional checks; some checks gave little signal. Forecasters with Brier worse than 0.25 excluded.
limits: Correlation across a few forecasters; better models are both more consistent and more accurate, so part is shared cause. Some consistency checks fail.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-computable check (G3 style, held-out symmetry) with no ground truth. Which checks to use matters; test before trusting.

source: Turtel, Franklin and Schoenegger (2025) LLMs can teach themselves to better predict the future
finding: Fine-tuning on the model's own reasoning ranked by outcomes lifted small-model forecasts to near GPT-4o.
numbers: 12,100 Polymarket questions; test after 2024-12-25. Phi-4 14B Brier 0.200 vs base 0.221 and random-label control 0.214. DeepSeek-R1 14B 0.197 vs base 0.211 and control 0.212. Gain 7-10% accuracy.
limits: Training, not scaffold; short test window; prediction-market questions with a known price.
agent_relevance: Training route is out of scope, but note the control: random labels gave a small gain too (0.221 to 0.214), so some benefit is exposure not learning.

source: Hsieh, Fu and Chen (2024) Reasoning and tools for human-level forecasting (RTF)
finding: A tool-using agent loop matched a Manifold-market crowd on two-week questions; ensembling helped agents but not base models.
numbers: Crowd Brier 0.172, accuracy 73.8%. RTF median-of-3 0.169; mean-of-3 0.170 (73.9%); sampled single run 0.180. Base GPT-4o ensemble 0.218 vs single 0.210 (ensemble worse). Ensemble SD 0.092 for agents vs 0.150 for base models.
limits: Short-horizon questions; small test; crowd is a market price with noise.
agent_relevance: Aggregation helps only when members are calibrated and less noisy; averaging noisy members can hurt. Check variance before voting.

source: Grove et al. (2000) via Mellers et al. (2024): clinical vs statistical prediction meta-analysis
finding: Statistical rules beat human intuition by a small but steady margin across many domains. Cited, not opened.
numbers: d = 0.12 (as reported in Mellers et al.).
limits: Not opened. Mostly non-geopolitical tasks with plentiful data.
agent_relevance: Code should make the final aggregation step; the effect is small, so do not expect large gains from this alone.

source: Tetlock (2005) Expert political judgment, via Mandel and Barnes (2014)
finding: Founding study: experts' long-range political forecasts were poorly calibrated and overconfident. Cited, not opened.
numbers: Best forecasters in the sample explained about 20% of outcome variance (per Mandel and Barnes).
limits: Not opened. Long horizons, no accountability; Tetlock and Mellers say it does not show analysts are incorrigibly miscalibrated.
agent_relevance: Baseline for 'expert vs chance'. The sign of miscalibration flips across settings, so test per setting.

source: Baron, Mellers, Tetlock, Stone and Ungar (2014) Two reasons to make aggregated probability forecasts more extreme, Decision Analysis 11
finding: Averaged forecasts should be pushed toward 0 and 1 because the crowd shares information and individuals are underconfident. Cited, not opened.
numbers: Reported as improving calibration in IARPA ACE (cited in Mandel and Tetlock 2018).
limits: Not opened. Our guardrail G4 forbids extremizing votes from one model, where samples are not independent.
agent_relevance: Extremizing is valid only for diverse, independent forecasters. For one model's samples it would overstate confidence.
